items.title: Beyond a Moratorium: Toward a Competency-Based Approach to AI Governance
items.summary: As state legislatures across the country prepare to convene in early 2026, a predictable panic is setting in among the architects of the artificial-intelligence (AI) revolution. From Sacramento to Hartford, legislation appears certain to proliferate seeking to regulate everything from algorithmic discrimination to the fundamental compute power used to train large language models (LLMs). The industry response has been equally predictable: a desperate plea for federal preemption, a moratorium on state action, or an aspirational reliance upon the Dormant Commerce Clause to strike down fractured compliance regimes. While legally plausible, we’ve seen over the past week that this lobbying strategy is fraught with political risk for the long-term viability of AI governance. It is true that a patchwork of 50 contradictory AI regimes would be an economic nightmare that could stifle U.S. innovation. And it is equally true that, under Dormant Commerce Clause jurisprudence, states cannot unduly burden interstate commerce or regulate conduct that occurs wholly outside their borders. But waiting for a gridlocked Congress to pass a sweeping preemption bill, or hoping the courts will briskly invalidate state laws, is a gamble on a timeline that fast-paced AI innovation and a race to beat our international peers and adversaries does not afford. The debate has become stuck in a binary trap: total federal control versus chaotic state experimentation. Against the backdrop of these choices, we need to take seriously the idea that the still-in-progress AI revolution (which, in truth, comprises an incredibly broad array of tools and technologies) requires nuanced and diverse approaches to deal with both its promises and its perils. What we really need is a new conceptual framework—one grounded not just in constitutional law, but in the practical reality of regulatory competency. The path forward isn’t to ask whether states can regulate AI, but to rigorously define what states are competent to regulate. This approach requires a return to the principle of subsidiarity—the idea that governance should occur at the level most capable of effectively addressing a specific issue. In the context of AI, this forces us to ask a difficult question: What harms are states actually capable of preventing, and what regulatory tools do they possess that will not inevitably spill over into the sovereignty of their neighbors? Consider the nature of the technology. The development of foundational models—the massive, compute-intensive training of systems like GPT-4 or Claude—is an inherently national, if not global, enterprise. The physical infrastructure, data flows, and capital investment ignore state lines. When a state attempts to regulate the training of these models (as seen in recent ambitious proposals), they are asserting a regulatory competency they simply do not possess. A state legislature inevitably lacks the technical capacity to audit the weights of a neural network effectively. Moreover, any attempt to impose safety standards on model training in one state inevitably dictates the technological architecture for the entire nation. This is the classic “California Effect,” where one jurisdiction’s policy preferences become a de facto national mandate, bypassing the democratic preferences of citizens in Texas or Ohio. This is where the Dormant Commerce Clause argument is strongest, but also where it is the most politically brittle. Telling a state legislator they cannot protect their constituents from “AI risks” because of an abstract constitutional doctrine reads as evasion. A better argument—and a better policy—is to channel state energies toward where their competency actually lies: the specific application of AI modalities within their particular jurisdictions. For example, states are eminently competent to regulate how their own government agencies use AI. They can and should set rules on how local police departments use facial recognition, or how state benefit agencies use automated decisionmaking systems to determine eligibility for Medicaid. These are local contexts involving local actors, and the redress (administrative hearings, tort liability) is well within the traditional state police power. Furthermore, states have a valid role in regulating the outputs of AI where they intersect with existing state laws and cause demonstrable harm. If an AI system is used to make hiring decisions in New York, it must comply with New York’s employment-discrimination statutes. If a chatbot gives medical advice in Florida, it touches upon Florida’s medical-licensing regime. In these instances, the state is not regulating the architecture of the AI—an area where they lack competency—but rather the conduct of the deployer, an area where they have centuries of experience. Previous episodes in tech policy demonstrate how this works. The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals’ decision in Fair Housing Council v. Roommates.com offers a helpful structural analogy. That case asked whether Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act foreclosed state enforcement of fair-housing laws against an online roommate-matching service. While the holding ultimately turned on the statutory limits of Section 230—specifically, that the platform had materially contributed to the unlawful conduct—the result is instructive. It demonstrates how federal law governing aspects of online infrastructure does not automatically insulate downstream conduct from state civil-rights enforcement. The Roommates case was not about federalism per se , but it reflects a similar subsidiarity logic: a federal rule can set the background architecture of an online system, while states retain authority to police discriminatory outcomes within their traditional domains. That division of labor is a useful mental model for thinking about AI governance. The distinction between fundamental development of AI and the behavior of AI systems is crucial. When states focus on conduct and outcomes within their borders, they allow for a healthy laboratory of democracy. For better or worse, one state might prefer a strict liability regime for automated-vehicle accidents; another might prefer a negligence standard to encourage automated-vehicle adoption. These differences reflect local risk tolerances and preferences. They do not break the internet, nor do they force a developer in Seattle to recode their model to suit a regulator in Tallahassee. But when states attempt to regulate the design and development of the technology itself—requiring predeployment impact assessments for general-purpose models, or mandating specific watermarking technicalities—they step outside their zone of competency. They move from governing local behavior to governing the interstate market for computation. The industry’s path forward should not be a blanket “No” to any state role, but a nuanced “Here, not there.” We must concede that states have a duty to police the specific harms that occur within their boundaries. These harms may relate to bias in housing, privacy in public spaces, preventing fraud and other torts, and the administration of state justice. In exchange, we must insist that the technology’s architecture—the “code” of the AI itself—remains the domain of federal oversight—or, better yet, competitive market standards. Our normative preferences about how any individual state chooses to wield its police powers will inevitably diverge. Even so, it is essential to preserve space for states to exercise those traditional authorities where they are most effective. The purpose of a new federal framework for AI should not be to displace state governance, but to ensure that AI systems can be created within a regulatory environment calibrated to their inherently interstate and international character. That division of labor protects innovation at the architectural layer, while respecting the states’ longstanding role in policing concrete harms that occur within their borders. By reframing the debate around subsidiarity and competency, we move past the stalemate of preemption. We acknowledge that states have a role, but cabin that role to where it is effective and legitimate. This would prevent the Balkanization of the digital economy while respecting the federalist impulse to keep governance close to the people. It is a harder argument to make than a simple slogan about innovation, but it is the only one likely to survive the political realities of the coming decade. The post Beyond a Moratorium: Toward a Competency-Based Approach to AI Governance appeared first on Truth on the Market .

items.title: The Irresistible Promise of Free Money
items.summary:
“People that are against Tariffs are FOOLS! We are now the Richest, Most Respected Country In the World, With Almost No Inflation, and A Record Stock Market Price. 401k’s are Highest EVER. We are taking in Trillions of Dollars and will soon begin paying down our ENORMOUS DEBT, $37 Trillion. Record Investment in the USA, plants and factories going up all over the place. A dividend of at least $2000 a person (not including high income people!) will be paid to everyone.” – President Donald J. Trump, November 9, 2025, TruthSocial Free Money! Politics is a dirty trade. To get elected, politicians must make promises they cannot possibly deliver. Then, once in office, they must somehow pretend to be delivering.

Giving away free money to people is one of the more popular devices. Typically, this is in the form of spending programs or tax credits. The objective is to redirect money to preferred areas of the economy – like defense or energy – and those who operate there.

On occasion, however, when the times call for it, politicians will mail out checks directly to people who didn’t earn them. These checks are above and beyond basic welfare and social security benefits. We saw this with Bush the Younger’s rebate checks and then with stimmy checks during the coronavirus fiasco. The news from Washington, particularly the recent announcement of a “tariff dividend” to be paid to the American people, is another example of political candy with a new twist. This time, a destructive tax is being depicted as an economic boon.

President Donald Trump is peddling the loot raised in U.S. tariff revenue. He presents it as a windfall from foreign nations. He’s proposing to take this revenue and distribute it as $2,000 checks . He calls it a “dividend,” and plans to send it out around July 2026 – just in time for the mid-term elections. He also claims this will somehow reduce the national debt.

This is a fine example of the “seen and the unseen” error that’s ignored in public economic discourse. Billions in tariff revenue enter the Treasury. We are told this is new wealth that can be freely disbursed. This is the seen.

What is unseen is the actual, destructive cost of obtaining this revenue through tariffs and the inevitable consequences of distributing that money back into the economy in the form of mass payments. A Tax on the American Consumer To be clear, tariffs are not a punishment inflicted upon foreign nations that they alone absorb. A tariff is a tax on the importing citizens of the nation that imposes it.

For example, when the government levies a tax on imported washing machines, that tax must be paid by someone. But who?

Initially, the importer pays it to the customs authorities. But it doesn’t start and end there. Remember, business is not a charitable endeavor. When providing goods or services, businesses must earn a profit. To remain solvent, the importer must pass this cost along.

In this example, they sell the washing machine to the retailer at a higher price. The retailer, in turn, sells it to the American consumer – that’s you – at a higher price.

At best, the final price of the imported good is inflated by the full amount of the tariff. We say at best because when protectionist games are being played, domestic producers of competing goods are afforded an artificial cushion. They are incentivized to raise their own prices.

Tariffs acts as a general sales tax levied on specific goods. This tax primarily burdens low-income families who spend a larger percentage of their earnings on essential goods.

Customs duties collected in fiscal year 2025 came to $195 billion . In fiscal year 2026, this may rise to around $300 billion. Regardless, the tariff revenue the government collects is not a “dividend” from China or Mexico. It’s hundreds of billions extracted from the pockets of American consumers and producers.

Tariff revenue represents hundreds of billions in higher costs for materials, tools, and finished goods, making American industry less competitive and diminishing the real wages of every worker.

To celebrate this revenue is to celebrate a self-imposed national decline in real purchasing power. The Destructive Nature of Protectionism Beyond elevating prices, tariffs are destructive to the natural flow of the economy. They are a tool central planners use to artificially guide capital and labor into industries where, without protection, they would not succeed.

Tariffs are policies of protectionism. They aim to save domestic jobs in high-cost, inefficient industries from competition. However, resources are not infinite. To keep one inefficient industry alive by force of law requires drawing capital, labor, and talent away from other, more efficient, wealth-creating industries.

Tariffs, for example, may save 1,000 jobs in the steel industry. But, in return, 5,000 jobs are lost in industries that use steel – such as construction, manufacturing, and automobiles – because their material costs have been artificially raised. This makes their final products more expensive and less competitive within the U.S. and with foreign trading partners.

Tariffs, in short, subtract wealth. They do not add to it. They make the nation poorer, not richer, by subsidizing inefficiency and penalizing productivity. The idea that we can grow rich and pay down the debt by intentionally preventing ourselves from buying goods at the lowest available price is absurd and has been refuted for centuries.

The other absurdity, however, is the proposed “dividend” distribution. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget estimates this plan could cost $600 billion, which is double the tariff revenue projected for fiscal year 2026.

If the payout were equal to the projected revenue – say, $300 billion – the government has merely collected $300 billion from the American people via the tariff-tax and handed it straight back to them. American citizens have not gained anything in aggregate.

The tariffs’ destructive, distorting effect on trade and production remains. The cost of goods remains high, and the overall economy is still poorer than it would have been under free trade.

But the payout is not equal to the projected revenue. It’s double ($600 billion!). This is where President Trump’s promise to reduce debt breaks down. A $600 billion expenditure against a $300 billion revenue stream means the government must borrow the additional $300 billion.

The claim that we’ll also pay down the debt while simultaneously proposing a $600 billion program based on only $300 billion in revenue doesn’t add up. But that’s not all… The Irresistible Promise of Free Money The act of dumping $600 billion dollars back into the economy as government sponsored consumption stimulus checks, even if partially offset by tariffs, will further the inflation problem. Yet, that is the very problem the checks are supposed to solve.

People are frustrated with the high cost of living. They want more money. But what causes the cost of living to rise?

Too much money chasing too few goods.

The tariffs restrict the supply of goods by penalizing imports and distorting domestic production. Then, the dividend checks inject a massive surge of new purchasing power (some of it borrowed) into the hands of consumers.

Tariffs, followed by tariff dividend checks, limit the supply of goods while simultaneously inflating demand. This is a plan that promises relief while, in effect, it accelerates the very inflation that consumers are being destroyed by.

In short, a tariff dividend is not a dividend at all. It’s a refund of an economically damaging tax. Moreover, this refund will be partially financed with debt.

Ultimately, you can’t get something for nothing. The wealth of a nation is generated by production, efficiency, and the division of labor that is best facilitated by free exchange. Tariffs, on the other hand, destroy wealth.

Paying the tariff revenue back to the people simply redistributes a net loss. What’s more, it finances that distribution through deeper debt and currency debasement.

So, why do it?

Like all government programs, it comes down to politics. Tariff dividend checks are great politics. Trump is a great politician.

The promise of free money for the majority of Americans is simply irresistible. And in a democracy, where the mob rules, that’s what counts.
